utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are in session. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. In order to continue the cross-examination of the present witness, we will move into closed session. Before we'll hear the testimony of the next witness, also in closed session, there are a few procedural matters I'd like to raise and which we prefer to deal with before we start with the next witness. There are a few other procedural matters which might have to wait until Thursday, most likely we'll have some time left Thursday for procedural matters. And we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would like to deliver a short decision on the admission of intercepts tendered through Witness JF-002. On the 11th of October, 2010, the Trial Chamber received submissions from the parties regarding the admissibility of intercepts tendered through Witness JF-002. Having considered those submissions, the Trial Chamber decides to admit those intercepts to which the Defence raised no objections. These were MFIs P619 through 670, and MFIs 672 through 715, as well as the intercept authentification spreadsheet MFI P618. The Trial Chamber admits these documents into evidence. And if there's any need, Mr. Groome, to have any of them under seal, the Chamber would like to be informed as soon as possible so that it finally can attribute either status of a public document or under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we hear from you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can do that before the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the end of the week. Madam Registrar, therefore, the -- these documents, although admitted, have not yet received the status of public documents, and Mr. Groome will revisit the matter by the end of this week, which means by -- would that be tomorrow, Mr. Groome? The end of the week on paper ends on Friday; in court, it ends on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was thinking Friday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then you will make submissions in a way appropriate to the content of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the submissions by the Prosecution, the Prosecution indicated that it would further follow up with the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the intercept MFI P671 and the related intercept monitor note MFI'd P716. The Trial Chamber will delay its ruling on these two documents. And this concludes the decision of the Chamber. The next item I would like to briefly touch upon is scheduling issues. I already briefly raised yesterday in court the concerns of the Chamber in relation to the scheduling of witnesses, also in view of the most recent medical reports the Chamber received. Three items. The first one, next week commencing 15th of November, Mr. Groome, three witnesses are scheduled for that week: Mr. Kirudja, still to be cross-examined by the Simatovic Defence; Witness JF-030; and JF-053. The Chamber wondered whether it is a realistic scheduling. But before going into any further detail, the Chamber would like to know what the estimates are, Defence estimates, for the time needed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could say on this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- Mr. Jordash has very helpfully given us estimates after this last notification was given out for the remainder of the case, and we have included them in this week's notification. And based on that, I think it's clear that the schedule as notified last week is unrealistic, and we are revising it today. We have not heard from the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if the Simatovic Defence would also provide relevant information to Mr. Groome so as to enable him to review his scheduling and the assessments on which they are based.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will provide our own assessments by the end of this week for the time needed for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps for the cross-examination of Mr. Kirudja it would be helpful to already have that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Mr. Kirudja is concerned, we will need up to an hour. About an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I also indicate that I'll be applying for leave to re-open cross-examination for Mr. Kirudja to put to Mr. Kirudja some issues relating to the UN hostage crisis. We've received documents and -- since we cross-examined Mr. Kirudja, and I think it would be useful if we were able to cross-examine him for up to an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the application is on the record now. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I've indicated to Mr. Jordash that I would not be opposing that application; he explained his reasons for me. And if the Chamber would feel that it would assist the Chamber hearing Mr. Kirudja on these points, the Prosecution will not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, you will, in anticipation of the Chamber approving where the parties seem to agree on appropriately further cross-examining Mr. Kirudja, that you include that in your reconsideration of the scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But if I could just say one thing. With respect, it's very -- with this issue, it's very helpful to have the estimates. Of course, it's only -- it's more helpful if we have some indication from the Chamber that it is going to adopt the time requested or is it going to make its own decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I was asking for the -- and then you intervened and you said you received information from Mr. Jordash. But what that information, apart from Mr. Kirudja, is is still unknown to the Chamber. Therefore, if you want the Chamber to look at it, then we need to receive that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And could I ask that for next week - and it seems that we'll have that information by the end of the week for the rest of the case, the rest of the Prosecution case - could I ask that we -- counsel inform the Chamber with respect to next week and it would greatly assist the Prosecution in revising next week to know approximately what times will be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps we should not wait until Friday with that. Mr. Petrovic, I'm talking about next week witnesses only. You've informed us about Mr. Kirudja. Then for witnesses JF-030 and JF-053, the Chamber would like to receive your assessment by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate it if we may do it tomorrow, if that's not too late for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That should be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I said we'd like to receive it by tomorrow, so that's -- unless you have another tomorrow on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, of course not. I wasn't following the transcript, and I just saw what you said. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're on this issue, I could just finally just recognise from the Prosecution's point of view that the extra efforts that the Chamber has made to schedule additional hearings and to facilitate witnesses that have been scheduled to remain on schedule is not only greatly appreciated by the Prosecution but by the witnesses as well. And I also thank not only the Defence but the accused themselves for being flexible in the scheduling of hearings for the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record. I would like now to address the week of the 22nd of November. The Chamber has been copied, Chamber staff has been copied, on an e-mail exchanges on the scheduling of the witness of the 22nd of November, and one of the things we find -- found in this e-mail exchange is that the parties wanted to discuss the matters, and the Chamber wonders whether you'll find a solution to these scheduling difficulties in the week commencing the 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we did not discuss that. We are going to discuss it during the first break - Mr. Groome and our Defence team, that is - so we will be in a position to inform you after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Then the last scheduling item would be the week commencing the 6th of December where the expert testimony of Christian Nielsen has been scheduled. Mr. Groome, you've indicated that you sought to schedule this witness for five days which during that week, if I'm not mistaken, I earlier made reference to the medical reports. We have speeded up the trial by going from two days to three and then to four days, and it -- the Chamber has great hesitations to already in advance schedule a week for five days, also in view of the medical reports relating to Mr. Stanisic. But before we decide on that matter, is there any estimate yet? I take it then, Mr. Jordash, from your part there is. How much time you would need in cross-examination of Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We've indicated, I think, 8 to 10 hours, a similar amount as we took with Mr. Theunens. And may I also say this at this stage, that we find ourselves in slightly awkward circumstances in that Mr. Stanisic is determined to push on and in my view, based on the medical evidence and based on my own observations, sometimes to his own medical detriment. And so I put it in that way. I hope Your Honours understand the dilemma that we as his representatives find ourselves once we push to four days a week and certainly to five. We have an accused who wants to be cooperative and wants to be seen to be cooperative, but on the other hand we as Defence counsel have a job to do which is not always consistent with that determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have the medical report, which, until now, say, well, four days a week slowly move to that. But that's -- at this moment, that's the assessment of the medical specialist. If Mr. Stanisic would want to go to five days a week, then I can't say in advance that the Chamber would agree with that. Certainly not, because we are guided by the position taken by Mr. Stanisic, we are guided by the medical reports we receive, we are guided by our -- of course our personal impression on these days. I'm not saying that you say that he wants to go to five days a week, but I just explain our hesitation to go beyond anything which we find at this moment as an appropriate scheduling in the medical reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I certainly didn't wish to give the impression that we as the Defence accept that the four days a week indicated by the doctors is a realistic assessment in all instances. We filed our submissions on this point and Your Honours will be aware of those submissions and we do not move from those submissions which effectively in a nutshell were that the doctor's assessments was not based on the out-of-court work that we, the Defence, have to do with Mr. Stanisic and that he himself has to do to be fully up to speed on the court process and what's happening in the court. But what I was trying to say is that when we -- when we move to four days, Mr. Stanisic's instinct is always to say yes. And if we were to move to five, his instinct is always to say yes. And the point I was trying to make was that that instinct and that determination to be co-operative is not always consistent with my own observations or certainly not medical evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. You are telling us more or less that your personal assessment and appreciation of the condition does not always coincide with what Mr. Stanisic presents to us as what he would prefer to do if we improved -- if we scheduled beyond what we did in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think the subjects we're dealing with are complex, and the concentration required is significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's exhausting for all, especially those who are not of ordinary, normal health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's good that we have again got this clear explanation of your position, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Bakrac, cross-examination for Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, your first question had to do with Mr. Nielsen, so the position of our Defence is that we are going to need as much time that we had used for expert witness Theunens, that is to say, about ten hours, as far as I can remember. That is the amount of time that we used for Theunens. Another thing that I would like to mention, and I see that we are getting close to the time for the break. I hope that you will give me two or three minutes though. I would just like to remind the Trial Chamber of our motion when the modality of the trial was being changed, when we presented the problems that we were facing. Of course they are not of a health nature, they have nothing to do with our client's health, but they are of a different nature, and you are aware of that. And there is, therefore, no need for me to repeat that. We have made every effort and shall continue to do so to be co-operative, to not create problems for the Trial Chamber, for this trial to proceed as efficiently as possible without jeopardising the interest of our client and his right to a fair trial. In view of all the circumstances that you are aware of, we would not like to be brought into a situation akin to the one that happened last week. With the best of intentions of accommodating the schedule that the Prosecution, and may I say this once again, unintentionally, I'm sure, made in an unrealistic fashion, due to the seriousness and the volume of material involved with the testimony of Mr. Theunens, we simply didn't have time to prepare for the next witness. We have already said that a three-day working week does leave us some scope for catching up with the proceedings, but increasing the number of working days in court would reduce our possibility of dealing with our own client and looking through the material that we did not have time to look at since October, that is, when we got involved. With three days, we could catch up, and that would be the case until winter recess starts, and then we will not be in a position not to have a enough time to deal with a particular witness. After that, if the Prosecutor wants to bring some more witnesses, we would be prepared for them as well. What I'm trying to say is that I'm afraid that increasing the number of working days could bring us to a situation to appear before this Trial Chamber and say, yet again, that we were physically incapable of preparing for a witness. Our Defence team really doesn't want to be in that position. We are trying to be co-operative to a maximum and to help these proceedings evolve as speedily as possible without jeopardising the right of our client to a fair trial. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Groome, whatever the situation is, sitting three days a week or four days a week, it seems that if the Chamber would follow the assessment of the Defence in relation to Mr. Nielsen, and I'm therefore returning to the week of the 6th of December, that it would be unrealistic to expect that the testimony of Mr. Nielsen would be concluded in one week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honour, and I will make contact with Mr. Nielsen and get information about his availability both the remainder of December and in January and provide that in the future weekly notification so the Chamber will hopefully have more -- enough information to make decisions about when he would like to schedule his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. This, in order not to be misunderstood, is not a final ruling on granting the time the Defence claims for the cross-examination -- it claims they need for the cross-examination of Mr. Nielsen, let me be clear. We will have a break. Could I also hear from the Defence how much time they would need for the cross-examination of the next -- no, no, let me first ... Talking about the next witness, Mr. Bakrac, a minute ago you referred to the testimony of Mr. Theunens and you also refer to not having had sufficient time to prepare for the next witness. I understood that to be that you didn't -- that you referred to a situation in the past where you had not sufficient time to prepare for the witness who was called as the first after Mr. Theunens had testified, and not for the next witness, that is, the witness who will start his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was not very specific, but I fully understand that you want to have a clear situation in the transcript. Precisely. I was talking about the witness who followed Witness Theunens. I was not talking about the next Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is understood. Could I hear from the Defence how much time they would need for the cross-examination of Witness JF-004 who will testify in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It depends. It would be between 30 minutes and one hour, depending upon a legal argument which we need to make concerning additional evidence served yesterday. If Your Honours rule that evidence inadmissible, it will be approximately 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and this is an invitation already, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Accidently made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am prepared for the next witness, but if Mr. Jordash covers what I think he will cover, our Defence most probably will not have any questions for JF-004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, this even perhaps opens an opportunity that we would conclude that testimony today, because you need how much?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Estimated about an hour and a half for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hour and a half, yes. Well, and hour and a half plus one hour is two hours and a half, is two times 75 minutes. But even if we would conclude with the testimony of the next witness today, the Chamber nevertheless would like to briefly deal with a few procedural matters which have been pending and have been delayed for quite a while. So, therefore, even if you would hurry to conclude the testimony today, don't be yet convinced that there would be not even a short session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think there also may be legal submissions with respect to some of the evidence, judging from our discussions with Mr. Jordash earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think matters are clear at this moment that we might easily conclude the testimony of the next witness this week, and most likely we need part of tomorrow's session for dealing with all the matters on our desk at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in those circumstances, Mr. Stanisic would request to be excused tomorrow. He's in the middle of some serious medical examinations. The first part took -- occurred this morning, and the second part would be tomorrow. So his request would be to be excused from court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be very clear, the medical situation of Mr. Stanisic is not such that he says, Please have no hearing tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, he's -- it's really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He will then waive his right to be present in court tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he would waive his right. I think he's fairly exhausted by the examinations, but he's content with the court proceeding, whether we finish with the witness or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it may be clear that we would seriously consider any application under the present circumstances to adjourn until these reasons do not exist anymore for not attending.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic requested that I make the application for him not to be present and indicated immediately he wanted the court proceedings to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear on the record. If there's nothing else, we'll have a break. And we resume at 4.00, and we'll then immediately turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into closed session in order to hear the evidence of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just check that -- I cannot remember whether Your Honours agreed that Mr. Stanisic could be absent tomorrow, so I just wanted to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether I expressly said so, but that the Chamber agrees that Mr. Stanisic can be absent tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the request is still there, although we have moved a bit slower with the evidence of the present witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The position remains the same. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, where the spreadsheet was admitted confidentially, that the -- none of the transcripts of the video -- of the intercepted telephone conversations, that there's no need to keep them confidential?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour; they can all be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. All public. We adjourn for the day. And we'll resume tomorrow, the 11th of November, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in this same Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of November, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
